p.src: One morning, when Gregor Samsa awoke from troubled dreams, he discovered that he had been transformed in his bed into a gigantic poisonous insect. He lay on his armor-hard back, and when he raised his head a little, he saw his brown belly, domed and divided into several curved ridges. The bedcover was about to slide completely off the mound of his belly and was only just holding on. His many legs, pitifully thin compared with their usual size, glimmered forlornly before his eyes. “What has happened to me?” he wondered. It was no dream. His room—a proper room, though a little too small—stood within the four familiar walls. Unpacked samples of cloth lay spread out on the table—Samsa was a traveling salesman—and on the wall above the table hung a photograph. He had cut it out of an illustrated magazine only recently and placed it in a handsome gilt frame. The photograph showed a lady wearing a fur hat and fur stole, sitting upright and holding out toward the viewer a heavy fur muff that completely concealed her arms up to the elbows. Gregor’s gaze then turned toward the window. The gloomy weather—he could hear raindrops striking the metal window ledge—made him thoroughly melancholy. “What if I slept a little longer and forgot all this nonsense?” he thought, but that proved utterly impossible. For he was accustomed to sleeping on his right side, but in his present condition he could not assume that position.

p.src: “Ah, what an exhausting profession I’ve chosen,” he thought. “Day in, day out, I’m on the road. The strain of doing business is far greater than it would be in a regular job at home, and on top of that there are all the hardships of travel. Making train connections, irregular and miserable meals, dealing constantly with different people so that no relationship lasts and no one can ever become truly close. Damn it all!” He felt a slight itch on his belly and, still lying on his back, slowly shifted himself toward the bedpost so that he could raise his head more easily, then found the itching spot. The spot was covered only with small white flecks, and he could not tell what they were. He tried to touch the spot with one leg, but immediately drew it back. The touch sent a shudder through his body. He returned to his former position. “Getting up so early,” he thought, “makes a person completely witless. A person has to get enough sleep. The other salesmen live like women in a harem. For instance, when I return to the inn in the middle of the morning to write up the orders I’ve obtained, those fellows are only just sitting down at the breakfast table. I’d like to see what my employer would say if I tried that. I’d be dismissed on the spot. And yet, who knows whether that might not be the best thing for me? If I weren’t holding back for my parents’ sake, I would have resigned long ago.

p.src: He would have stepped up to his employer and poured out everything he felt from the bottom of his heart. His employer would surely have been so astonished that he fell off his desk! Sitting on top of a desk and speaking down to an employee from that height was a strange way of doing things. What was more, since the employer was hard of hearing, the employee had to come right up close to him. Well, he had not yet abandoned all hope. Once he had saved enough money to pay off his parents' entire debt to his employer—though that would still take another five or six years—he would certainly do it. For the moment, however, he first had to get up. My train leaves at five." Then he looked toward the alarm clock ticking on top of the chest of drawers. "Damn it!" he thought. It was already half past six, and the hands were moving calmly onward. It was past the half hour already and drawing close to a quarter to seven. Could the alarm have failed to ring? Even from the bed he could see that it had been properly set for four o'clock. It must have rung. But was it possible that he had slept peacefully through a peal loud enough to shake the furniture in the room? No, he had certainly not slept peacefully, but perhaps that was precisely why he had slept all the more deeply. But what was he to do now? The next train left at seven. To catch it, he would have to rush like a madman. And his sample collection was not yet packed, while he himself felt neither particularly well nor energetic. And even if he did catch the train, there would be no escaping his employer's wrath.

p.src: While he was thinking all this over in a frantic rush, still unable to resolve to leave the bed—the alarm clock had just struck twenty to seven—there came a knock at the door by the head of his bed. “Gregor,” the voice called—it was his mother—“it’s quarter to seven. Weren’t you going to leave?” Oh, that gentle voice! Gregor started when he heard his own voice answering. It was unmistakably his former voice, yet from somewhere deep beneath it came an uncontrollable, painfully squeaking sound. It allowed his words to retain their clarity only for the first instant, then so utterly ruined their resonance that one could not be sure they had been heard correctly. Gregor had wanted to answer at length and explain everything, but under the circumstances he confined himself to saying, “Yes, yes, I understand. Thank you, Mother. I’m getting up now.” The wooden door between them must have kept those outside from noticing the change in Gregor’s voice. For his mother was satisfied with this explanation and shuffled away. But this brief exchange alerted the rest of the family to the unexpected fact that Gregor was still at home. His father was already knocking on one of the side doors with his fist, though not very hard. “Gregor, Gregor,” his father called. “What in the world is the matter?” Then, after a short pause, he called to him again in a deeper voice. “Gregor! Gregor!”

p.src: The chief reason was that his body was so extraordinarily broad. To raise himself, he would normally have used his arms and legs. But instead of human limbs, he had numerous little legs that moved incessantly in wildly different ways, and he was unable to control them. Whenever he finally tried to bend one of the legs, the first thing it did was stretch itself straight. And whenever he thought he had at last succeeded in making that leg do as he wished, all the others would meanwhile thrash about in the most painfully unruly commotion, as though they had been set free.

p.src: “At any rate, I mustn’t stay in bed doing nothing,” Gregor told himself. First he tried to move the lower part of his body out of bed, but this lower portion, which he had not yet seen and could not form any accurate idea of, proved extremely difficult to move. He made progress only very slowly. At last, almost frantic, he gathered his strength and thrust his body recklessly forward; but he misjudged the direction and struck the bedpost at the foot of the bed with tremendous force, and the pain he felt taught him that the lower part of his body was, for the moment, its most sensitive region. So he tried instead to get the upper part of his body out of bed first, cautiously turning his head toward the edge. This worked just as he had hoped, and despite its great breadth and weight, his whole body at last slowly followed the turn of his head. But when at last his head was suspended in midair beyond the bed, he became afraid to move any farther forward in this manner. For if he ultimately let his body fall like this, only a miracle could keep him from injuring his head. And now, of all times, he must not lose his composure, whatever happened. So he decided that he would rather remain in bed.

But presently he told himself: “Before the clock strikes a quarter past seven, I absolutely must be completely out of bed. Besides, by then someone from the office will have come to ask about me. The office opens before seven.” This time he set about getting out of bed by rocking his entire body sideways in one steady, even motion. If he fell out of bed this way, he thought he could keep his head sharply raised as he dropped, and would therefore probably avoid injuring it. His back seemed hard. So it surely would not be hurt when he landed on the carpet. What worried him most was the tremendous noise he was bound to make when he fell. Behind every door, that noise would surely cause concern, even if it did not actually frighten anyone. Still, he had to take the risk. When Gregor was already hanging halfway out of bed—the new method was more like a game than an arduous task, for he needed only to keep rocking himself at intervals—it suddenly occurred to him how simple everything would be if someone came to help him.

p.src: “Madam, I can think of no other explanation either,” said the chief clerk. “I hope it is nothing serious. Still, we businessmen—whether fortunately or unfortunately, as the case may be—often have to overcome a slight indisposition without a second thought, for the sake of business.” “Then may we let the chief clerk in?” his impatient father asked, knocking on the door again. “No,” said Gregor. An awkward silence fell in the room to his left. In the room to his right, his sister began to sob. Why did his sister not join the others? She had probably only just got out of bed and had not even begun to dress. And why was she crying, anyway? Because he would not get up and would not let the chief clerk into his room? Because he was in danger of losing his position, whereupon his employer would bring up the old debts and hound his parents once again? But for the moment, such worries were unnecessary. Gregor was still here, and he had not the slightest thought of abandoning his family. For now he was lying quite comfortably on the carpet, and no one who knew his condition could seriously demand that he let the chief clerk into the room. And Gregor could not possibly be dismissed at once merely for this minor discourtesy, for which a suitable excuse could easily be found later.

p.src: “Mr. Samsa,” the chief clerk now called out in a raised voice. “What is the matter with you? You barricade yourself in your room and answer with nothing but yes or no. I thought you were a calm, sensible man, but now you suddenly seem determined to parade some strange whim before us. This morning our employer did hint at what he thought might explain your absence—namely, the money recently entrusted to you for collection—but I practically pledged my word that this explanation could not possibly be correct and spoke up in your defense. But now that I see you displaying this incomprehensible obstinacy, I have not the slightest inclination to take your side. Besides, your position is by no means so secure. Please go now, chief clerk. I’ll come to the office myself at once. And please be so kind as to explain all this to the director.” Gregor rattled all this off in such haste that he scarcely knew what he was saying; yet, perhaps because of the practice he had already had in bed, he easily reached the chest of drawers and, clinging to it, tried to pull himself upright.

p.src: He truly meant to open the door, show himself, and speak to the chief clerk. He was consumed with curiosity to know what the people now so eager to see him would say when they caught sight of him. If they were horrified, then Gregor would no longer be responsible and could remain calm. If, on the other hand, they took it calmly, then he too would have no reason to become agitated and, if he hurried, could truly be at the station by eight. At first he slipped two or three times from the smooth chest of drawers, but at last, with one final leap, he managed to stand upright. The pain in the lower part of his body burned fiercely, but he no longer paid it any attention. Then he let his body fall against the back of a nearby chair and clung to its edge with his little legs. This enabled him to steady himself, and so he stopped speaking. For now he was able to listen to what the chief clerk was saying.

p.src: “Could you understand a single word your son said?” the chief clerk asked the parents. “Surely he isn't making fools of us?” “Good heavens, no!” cried his mother, already in tears. “He must be seriously ill. And here we are, tormenting him. Grete! Grete!” his mother called loudly. “What is it?” his sister called back from the other side. The two of them were speaking to each other across Gregor's room. “Go and fetch the doctor at once. Gregor is ill. Did you hear Gregor speaking just now?” “That sounded like the voice of an animal,” said the chief clerk, his voice conspicuously low compared with the mother's cries. “Anna! Anna!” his father shouted through the entrance hall toward the kitchen, clapping his hands. “Fetch a locksmith at once!” At once the two girls hurried through the entrance hall, their skirts rustling—how had his sister managed to dress so quickly?— and flung open the front door. There was no sound at all of the door closing. They must have left it wide open. That often happens in a household struck by great misfortune. Gregor, however, had grown much calmer. So people could no longer understand what he was saying. His words had seemed clear to him, clearer than before, but that was probably only because his ears had grown accustomed to them. Still, at least everyone now believed that something was wrong with him and was prepared to help him.

p.src: Gregor slowly made his way toward the door with the chair, then let go of it, threw himself against the door, and, clinging to it, raised himself upright—the little pads on the soles of his feet were slightly sticky. And there, for a moment, he rested from all his arduous exertions. Then he set about turning the key in the lock with his mouth. Unfortunately, he seemed to have nothing resembling teeth—how was he supposed to seize the key at once? On the other hand, his jaws were of course exceedingly strong, and with their help he did manage to move the key, though he failed to notice that he had undoubtedly injured some part of his body. The evidence of the injury was that a brown fluid flowed from his mouth, ran over the key, and dripped onto the floor. “Now, can’t you hear that?” said the chief clerk in the adjoining room. “He’s turning the key.” These words were a great encouragement to Gregor. But surely they should all have been cheering him on. His father and mother too. “Keep at it, Gregor. Come on! Hold tight to the key!” his parents too should have been shouting. Imagining that they were all watching his efforts with tense attention, he summoned every last bit of strength and bit down on the key until he nearly fainted. As the key continued to turn, he circled the lock as though dancing around it. By now, only his mouth was holding his body upright. As necessary, he would either hang from the key or press it downward again with the full weight of his body.

p.src: “So I didn’t need a locksmith after all.” Then, intending to open the door fully, he rested his head on the handle. Since this was how he had to open the door, the door was already quite far open before he himself could be seen from outside. First he had to edge slowly around the door panel. And he had to proceed cautiously if he did not want to fall flat on his back before entering the room. He was still wholly occupied with this difficult maneuver and had no time to pay attention to anything else when he heard the chief clerk cry out loudly, “Oh!” The cry sounded like the rushing of the wind. Then he saw the chief clerk as well: standing nearest the door, the man pressed a hand over his gaping mouth and slowly backed away, as though driven off by an invisible force of constant strength. His mother—despite the chief clerk’s presence, she stood there with her hair still unbound and disheveled from the night before—first clasped her hands and looked at his father, then took two steps toward Gregor and sank limply to the floor amid her skirts, which spread out around her. Her face drooped toward her breast and was completely hidden from view. His father clenched his fists with a hostile expression, as though he meant to drive Gregor back into his room. Then he looked uneasily around the living room, covered his eyes with both hands, and began to weep. His broad, sturdy-looking chest shook with sobs.

She had forgotten that the table laid for breakfast was behind her. p.src: Instead of going after the manager himself, or at least refraining from hindering Gregor as he tried to follow him, his father seized in his right hand the cane that the manager had left behind on a chair with his hat and overcoat, took a large newspaper from the table with his left, and began stamping his feet and brandishing the cane and newspaper to drive Gregor back into his room. No matter how much Gregor pleaded, it was no use; however insistently he begged, his father would not listen. However humbly he tried to turn his head, his father merely stamped his feet all the harder. Across the room, despite the cold weather, his mother had flung open a window and was leaning far out of it, her face buried in her hands. A powerful draft sprang up between the street and the stairwell; the window curtains billowed, the newspapers on the table rustled, and several sheets came apart and flew down onto the floor. His father drove him on relentlessly, hissing at him like a savage. Gregor, however, had never practiced moving backward, and in fact could make only painfully slow progress. If only Gregor could have turned around, he would have reached his room at once, but he was afraid that the laborious maneuver would irritate his father. Besides, at any moment the cane in his father's hand might deal him a fatal blow to the back or head. But in the end, he had no choice except to turn around.

p.src: For, to his astonishment, he discovered that while moving backward he could not keep to a straight course at all. So, constantly casting anxious sidelong glances at his father, he began to turn around as quickly as he could. In reality, however, he could carry out the maneuver only very slowly. Perhaps his father too recognized his good intentions. For he did not interfere with Gregor's movement, and from time to time, standing some distance away, he even seemed to direct the turning maneuver with the tip of his cane. If only his father had not kept up that unbearable hissing as he drove him on! Whenever Gregor heard it, he completely lost his composure. Even when he had almost finished turning around, the hissing would invariably distract and fluster him, so that he edged back a little toward his former position yet again. At last, however, he managed to bring his head to the doorway, only to discover that his body was too broad to pass through at once. In his present state of mind, it naturally never occurred to his father to open the other half of the double door and make enough room for Gregor to pass. His father had only one thought: to get Gregor back into his room as quickly as possible. Nor would his father ever have allowed Gregor the elaborate preparations he would have needed first to raise himself upright, though in that posture he might perhaps have been able to pass through the doorway.

p.src: Perhaps because there seemed to be no obstacle at all, his father was now making an extraordinary commotion as he drove Gregor onward. The sound Gregor heard behind him no longer seemed like the voice of his one and only father. And in truth, this was no longer a laughing matter. So Gregor, with a feeling of reckless abandon, forced his body into the doorway. One side of his body rose up, leaving him lodged diagonally in the doorway. One of his flanks was scraped completely raw, leaving a revolting stain on the white door. Soon he was wedged fast and could no longer move by himself. All the legs on one side of his body were suspended in the air, while those on the other side were pressed painfully against the floor. —Then, from behind, his father gave his body one powerful shove that now proved truly helpful. Gregor went flying far into the room, bleeding profusely. The door was then slammed shut with the cane, and at last everything fell silent.

p.src: In the dim light of dusk, Gregor finally awoke from a heavy, almost unconscious sleep. Surely, even if nothing had disturbed him, he would not have awakened so late. For he felt thoroughly rested and as though he had slept his fill. Yet it seemed to him that he had been awakened by quick footsteps and the sound of the door leading to the entrance hall being carefully closed. The light from the electric streetlamps cast a pale glow on the ceiling and the upper parts of the furniture, but down where Gregor lay, all around him was dark. Only now did he realize their value. Still probing clumsily with his antennae, he slowly shifted his body toward the door, intending to see what had happened there. The left side of his body felt like one long, unpleasantly taut wound, and he was forced to limp in earnest on the rows of little legs along both sides. One leg, moreover, had been seriously injured during the events of the morning—it was almost a miracle that only one had been hurt— and it trailed lifelessly behind him. Only when he reached the door did he understand what had drawn him there. It was the smell of something to eat. For there stood a bowl filled with sweetened milk, with a small piece of white bread floating in it. He was so delighted that he almost laughed aloud. He was even hungrier than he had been that morning and at once plunged his head into the milk almost up to his eyes. But before long he withdrew it in disappointment.

p.src: When Gregor peered through the crack in the door, he saw that the gas lamp was lit in the living room. Usually at this hour, his father would read the afternoon newspaper aloud to his mother, and sometimes to his sister as well, but now not a sound could be heard. These readings, which his sister had so often told him about in conversation and in her letters, had probably fallen almost entirely out of practice of late. Yet everything around him was utterly still, although the apartment surely could not be empty. “What a quiet life the family leads,” Gregor told himself, and as he stared into the darkness, he felt immensely proud that he had been able to provide his parents and sister with such a life in so fine a home. But what if all this peace, happiness, and contentment were now to end in horror? Rather than lose himself in such thoughts, Gregor set himself in motion and crawled back and forth across the room. During the long night, first one door and then the other opened a crack, only to be shut again at once. Someone must surely have had reason to enter the room, but their hesitation was simply too great. So Gregor stationed himself right beside the door leading to the living room, determined either to admit the hesitant visitor or at least to discover who it was. But the door did not open again, and Gregor waited in vain.

p.src: Only late that night was the light in the living room finally put out. It was therefore easy to tell that his parents and sister had remained awake all that time. For he could hear quite clearly how all three of them then tiptoed away. That meant no one would enter Gregor’s room again before morning. He therefore had plenty of time to consider, without interruption and at length, how he ought to arrange his life from now on. Yet the spacious, high-ceilinged room in which he was now forced to lie pressed flat against the floor filled him with unease, though he could not discover why. After all, he had lived in this room for five years, and he could not understand why it should make him feel this way. —And, turning almost unconsciously, though not without a slight feeling of shame, he hurried beneath the sofa. There, although his back was slightly compressed and he could no longer raise his head, he at once felt exceedingly comfortable. The only pity was that his body was too broad to fit completely beneath the sofa. He remained there throughout the night. He passed the night partly dozing, though hunger kept waking him, and partly absorbed in worries and vague hopes. But all these worries and hopes led to the same conclusion: for the present he must remain calm and, through patience and the utmost consideration, help his family endure the various discomforts he was bound to cause them.

p.src: Early the next morning, while it was still almost night, Gregor had an opportunity to test the resolve he had only just made. For his sister, almost fully dressed, opened the door from the hall and peered inside with a tense expression. She did not see him at once, but when she noticed him beneath the sofa—he had to be somewhere, after all. He could hardly have flown away—she was so startled that she lost her composure and slammed the door shut again from outside. But, as though regretting her behavior, she immediately opened the door again and tiptoed into the room as if she were visiting someone gravely ill or a complete stranger. Gregor stretched his head almost to the edge of the sofa and watched his sister. Would she notice that he had left the milk untouched? And it certainly was not because he lacked an appetite. Would she bring him some other food more suited to his taste? Would she do it of her own accord? He would rather starve to death than draw her attention to it. Even so, he was actually consumed by the desire to spring out from under the sofa, throw himself at his sister's feet, and beg her for something tasty to eat. His sister, however, immediately noticed the bowl of milk, which was still full, and looked puzzled. Only a little milk had spilled around the bowl. She picked up the bowl at once, though not with her bare hands, but with a rag. Then she carried the bowl out.

p.src: Gregor was intensely curious about what his sister might bring instead, and he imagined all manner of possibilities. Yet mere speculation could never have enabled him to guess what she actually brought out of kindness. To test his tastes, she had selected a variety of foods and spread them all out on an old newspaper. There were old, half-rotten vegetables; bones left over from supper, coated in congealed white sauce; a raisin or two and a few almonds; some cheese Gregor had declared inedible two days earlier; a slice of dry bread, a slice spread with butter, and a slice spread with butter and sprinkled with salt. Besides these, she set down a bowl that had apparently been designated for Gregor's exclusive use forevermore. It was filled with water. And because his sister knew that Gregor would not eat in her presence, she considerately hurried out of the room and even locked the door behind her. She did this to let Gregor understand that he could make himself comfortable and eat as he pleased. As Gregor set about his meal, his many little legs rustled and scraped. p.src: “Once again, no one has touched a thing.” Although Gregor could not hear the news directly, he picked up all sorts of things from the conversations in the adjoining rooms. Whenever he heard voices, he would hurry at once to the nearest door and press his whole body against it. Especially at first, there was not a single conversation, even if conducted only in whispers, that did not seem to concern him in some way. For two days, at every meal, he heard them discussing what they ought to do. And the same subject was discussed between meals as well. On the very first day, the maid too—though it was not at all clear what she knew about the incident, or how much—fell to her knees and begged his mother to dismiss her at once; and when she left the house fifteen minutes later, she thanked them through her tears for letting her go. Her manner suggested that this was the greatest kindness the household had ever shown her. And although no one had asked it of her, she swore with the utmost solemnity that she would not breathe a word of it to anyone.

On the very first day, the maid too—though it was not at all clear what she knew about the incident, or how much—fell to her knees and begged his mother to dismiss her at once; and when she left the house fifteen minutes later, she thanked them through her tears for letting her go.
Her manner suggested that this was the greatest kindness the household had ever shown her.
And although no one had asked it of her, she swore with the utmost solemnity that she would not breathe a word of it to anyone.

p.src: Now that the maid had left, Gregor’s sister had to help his mother with the cooking as well. Even so, it was not much work. After all, they ate almost nothing. Gregor repeatedly heard one of them urging another to eat, always without success; the only reply was invariably something like, “No, thank you, I’ve had enough.” Apparently, they drank no alcohol at all either. His sister would often ask their father whether he would like some beer, earnestly offering to fetch it herself; and when he remained silent, she would try to dispel any worry he might have about appearances by saying that they could have the porter’s wife fetch it instead. But at last their father would call out loudly, “I don’t want any.” After that, beer was not mentioned again. On the very first day, their father explained the family’s entire financial situation and its prospects to their mother and sister. From time to time he rose from the table and fetched some paper or account book from the small strongbox he had managed to salvage when his business failed five years earlier. They could hear him open the complicated lock and then close it again after taking out whatever he was looking for. In one respect, his father’s explanation gave Gregor the first cause for gladness since his confinement had begun. Until then, Gregor had believed that nothing at all had remained in his father’s hands from the old business. At least, his father had never told Gregor otherwise.

p.src: Still, Gregor had never asked his father about it. At that time, Gregor's sole concern had been to do everything in his power to make his family forget as quickly as possible the business misfortune that had plunged them all into utter despair. And so, at that time, he began working with exceptional zeal and rose almost overnight from an insignificant clerk to a traveling salesman. A salesman naturally had all sorts of opportunities to earn money, and the fruits of his labor could immediately be turned into cash in the form of commissions, which he could bring home and spread out on the table before his astonished and delighted family. Those were wonderful times. Later, Gregor still earned enough to meet the expenses of the entire household, and indeed did meet them, but those wonderful early days never returned, at least not with their former brilliance. His family and Gregor himself grew accustomed to it: they accepted the money gratefully, and he handed it over gladly, but that special warmth of feeling no longer arose. His secret plan was to send his sister, who unlike Gregor passionately loved music and could play the violin with moving skill, to the conservatory the following year. This was partly because he himself had long ceased to concern himself with such matters, and partly because Gregor's mother could not grasp everything at once after hearing it only once—and what Gregor learned was that, despite all their misfortunes, a portion of their former capital still remained, by no means an entirely negligible sum, and that the interest, left untouched, had meanwhile accumulated a little. Behind the door, Gregor nodded eagerly, delighted by this unexpected prudence and thrift.

p.src: He would often spend the entire long night on that sofa without sleeping for a moment, doing nothing but scratching at the leather for hours on end. Or else, undeterred by the tremendous effort it cost him, he would push a chair over to the window, crawl up onto the sill, and lean against the window while supporting himself on the chair. He seemed to be recalling the liberating feeling he had once experienced when looking out of the window. For in fact, with each passing day, even objects only a short distance away were growing increasingly blurred to his eyes. Even the hospital across the street, whose constant presence had once irritated him beyond endurance, had now vanished completely from sight. Had he not known perfectly well that he lived on Charlottenstrasse, a quiet yet thoroughly urban street, he might have believed that his window looked out upon a wasteland where the grey sky and grey earth merged indistinguishably into one another. His attentive sister must have noticed the chair standing by the window only twice, yet after that she always pushed it neatly back to the window once she had cleaned the room, and from then on she also left the inner window open.

p.src: If Gregor had been able to speak to his sister and thank her for everything she had to do for him, he could have accepted her ministrations more readily. But as it was, he found it unbearably painful. His sister, of course, did her best to erase every painful trace of the situation, and naturally grew more successful as time went on; but with time Gregor, too, came to perceive everything far more precisely than he had at first. The mere sound of his sister setting foot in the room filled him with dread. Although she normally took care not to let anyone see Gregor's room, the instant she entered she would not even take the time to close the door, but ran straight to the window, flung it open hurriedly with both hands as though she were suffocating, and then, however cold it might be, stood there for a while, breathing deeply. By rushing about and making such a commotion, she startled Gregor twice a day. All the while, he lay trembling beneath the sofa. Yet he knew very well that she would surely have preferred not to do this if only she could have endured keeping the window shut in a room where Gregor was present. One day, when a whole month had already passed since Gregor's transformation and his sister therefore no longer had any particular reason to be startled by his appearance, she came a little earlier than usual and found Gregor motionless, reared upright in a truly alarming posture, gazing out of the window.

p.src: Gregor would not have been surprised if his sister had simply refused to enter the room. After all, by holding himself in that position he was preventing her from opening the window at once. p.src: During the first two weeks, his parents could not bring themselves to enter his room. Gregor often heard his parents express their complete approval of his sister’s work now, though until then they had frequently been angry with her because they considered her a useless daughter. Indeed, while his sister was cleaning Gregor’s room, his parents would often wait together outside his door, and the moment she came out she had to tell them what the room looked like, what Gregor had eaten, how he had behaved, and whether there might perhaps have been some slight improvement in his condition. His mother, for her part, had wanted to visit Gregor fairly soon, but at first his father and sister restrained her by putting forward various reasonable arguments. Gregor listened to these arguments with the closest attention and considered every one of them entirely correct. Later, however, they had to hold his mother back by force. And when his restrained mother cried, “Let me go to Gregor! He is my poor son! Can’t you understand that I have to go to him?” Gregor thought that perhaps it would be better to let his mother come in—not every day, of course, but perhaps once a week. After all, his mother understood everything far better than his sister did. However brave his sister might be, she was still only a child and had ultimately taken on this difficult task out of childish thoughtlessness. Gregor’s wish to see his mother was soon fulfilled.

p.src: Out of consideration for his parents, Gregor had resolved not to go near the window during the day; yet there was little room to crawl about on the few square metres of floor, lying still was hard to endure even at night, and soon food no longer gave him the slightest pleasure, so for diversion he formed the habit of crawling back and forth across the walls and ceiling in every direction. He was especially fond of hanging from the ceiling. It was entirely different from lying motionless on the floor. He could breathe more freely, and a gentle vibration passed through his body. And sometimes, while Gregor hung from the ceiling in an almost blissful state of abstraction, he would let go with his legs, fall to the floor with a thud, and startle even himself. But by now, of course, he had far greater control over his body than before, and even such a great fall caused him no injury. His sister soon noticed this new amusement Gregor had discovered for himself—for as he crawled about, he left here and there traces of the sticky fluid exuded by his body—and she conceived the idea of giving him as much room as possible to crawl, by removing the furniture that obstructed him, above all the chest of drawers and the writing desk. But she could not do this work alone. She had no intention of asking her father for help, and the maid would certainly not be of much use either. For this girl of about sixteen, though she had bravely endured things since the former cook had given notice, had asked and received permission to keep the kitchen door locked at all times and to open it only when specially summoned.

p.src: And why should Gregor not feel the same way? He had been accustomed to the furniture in his room for so long that in an empty room he would surely feel abandoned. “Besides, if we do this,” their mother added at last, lowering her voice. Even before that she had been speaking almost in a whisper; though she did not know exactly where Gregor was, she seemed anxious to prevent even the sound of her voice from reaching him. His mother was convinced that Gregor could no longer understand human speech. “Besides, if we do this, won't removing the furniture be just like showing him that we have completely given up hope of his recovery and have abandoned him without another thought? I think it would be best if we tried to keep his room exactly as it was, so that when Gregor comes back to us he will see that nothing has changed and will find it all the easier to forget what has happened.” Hearing his mother's words, Gregor realized that the absence of any direct human conversation, combined with the monotonous life his family led, must have thoroughly confused his mind during these past two months. For there was no other way to explain how he could seriously have come to believe that it would be better for his room to be completely emptied. Did he really want to transform this warm room, so comfortably furnished with heirloom pieces, into a cavern?

The women were clearing out his room. They were taking away everything that had been familiar to him. The chest containing his fretsaw and other tools had already been carried away by the two of them. Now they were trying to loosen the desk that was firmly embedded in the floor. So he crawled out—the women were just then leaning against the desk in the adjoining room to catch their breath—and changed direction four times, utterly unable to decide what he should save first.

p.src: A little time passed. Gregor lay there utterly exhausted. Everything around him was utterly still. Surely that was a good sign. Then the bell at the front door rang. The maid was, of course, shut away in the kitchen, so Grete had to answer it. Their father had come home. “What has happened?” Those were his first words. Grete's appearance must have told him everything. Grete answered in a breathless voice, apparently with her face pressed against her father's chest. “Mother fainted. But she's all right now. Gregor crawled out.” “I knew this would happen,” said their father. “I was always warning you, but you women refuse to listen.” It was clear to Gregor that his father had misinterpreted Grete's all-too-brief report and concluded that Gregor had done something violent. Gregor therefore had to try to calm his father this time. For he had neither the time nor, indeed, the ability to explain matters to his father. So he fled to the door of his room and pressed himself tightly against it. That way, when his father entered from the hall, he ought to see at once that Gregor had the very best intention of returning immediately to his room, that there was therefore no need to drive him back, and that all anyone had to do was open the door and he would disappear inside at once. But his father was in no mood to notice such subtleties.

p.src: The moment he came in, he cried “Ah!” in a tone that seemed to mingle anger with delight— he cried. Gregor drew his head back from the doorway and raised it toward his father. He had truly never imagined his father as he now stood before him. Yet lately he had been so absorbed in his new manner of crawling about that he had neglected to pay attention to the other events in the household as he once had, and really ought to have been prepared to encounter domestic circumstances that had changed from what they used to be. Even so, could this still be his father? Could the aged father before him really be the same man who used to lie wearily sunk in bed when Gregor left on his business trips; who, on the evenings of Gregor’s return, would receive him from an armchair dressed in his nightclothes; who was wholly unable to rise and could show his pleasure only by lifting his arms; and who, on those rare walks they took together on one or two Sundays a year or on the great holidays, would stand between Gregor and his mother, slow walkers though they already were, and shuffle along even more slowly than they did, wrapped in his old overcoat and laboriously supporting himself on the crutch-topped cane he always planted carefully before him, almost invariably stopping whenever he wished to say something and gathering his companions around him? Unlike before, he now stood perfectly upright. He wore a close-fitting dark-blue uniform with gold buttons, like those worn by bank attendants.

p.src: Above the high, stiff collar of his coat spread a powerful double chin. Beneath his bushy eyebrows, his black eyes flashed with alert vitality. His white hair, usually disheveled, had been combed down into an exceedingly neat, glossy style. His father flung his peaked cap, which bore a gold-braided emblem that presumably belonged to the bank, in an arc across the whole room onto the sofa; then, throwing back the skirts of his long uniform coat and thrusting both hands into his trouser pockets, he advanced toward Gregor with a bitter expression. He surely did not know himself what he meant to do. In any case, he lifted his feet unusually high. Gregor was astonished at the enormous size of his boot soles. But he could not remain astonished. Ever since the first day of his new life, he had known perfectly well that his father considered only the utmost severity appropriate in dealing with him. So he fled from his father, stopping whenever his father stopped and scurrying forward again whenever his father moved. In this way they circled the room several times, but nothing decisive occurred; moreover, because the whole maneuver unfolded at so slow a pace, it did not look in the least like a pursuit. For the time being, therefore, Gregor remained on the floor. He was particularly afraid that if he fled onto the wall or ceiling, his father would take it as an act of peculiar malice. Nevertheless, he could not help telling himself that he would not be able to keep running about like this for long. For every single step his father took, he had to make countless movements.

p.src: He was already beginning to show clear signs of breathlessness. His lungs had never been particularly dependable even before. And so, trying to run with all his strength, he staggered and crawled about, his eyes scarcely open. Foolishly, he could think of no way to escape except by running. He had almost completely forgotten that he could move freely over the walls on every side. The walls, however, were obstructed by carefully carved furniture covered with projections and sharp points. —Just then, something gently tossed landed close beside him and rolled along the floor. It was an apple. A second one immediately flew toward him. Gregor stopped short in astonishment. There was no point in running any farther. For his father had resolved to bombard him. He had taken apples from the fruit bowl on the sideboard, stuffed his pockets full of them, and was now hurling them one after another, without yet taking very careful aim. The little red apples rolled about the floor as though electrified and collided with one another. One apple, thrown without much force, grazed Gregor's back and slid off without doing him any harm. But the very next one that flew at him lodged squarely in Gregor's back. As though the sudden, incredible pain might vanish if he changed position, Gregor tried to drag himself forward; but he felt as if he had been nailed to the spot, and collapsed with all his senses in utter confusion. With one last gaze, growing steadily dimmer, he saw the door of his room open and his mother rush out ahead of his screaming sister. She was in her underclothes.

p.src: The grave injury from which Gregor suffered for more than a month—the apple remained embedded in his flesh as a visible memento, since no one dared remove it—seemed to remind even his father that, despite Gregor's present pitiful and repulsive form, he was still a member of the family; that he must not be treated as an enemy; and that family duty required them to swallow their disgust and endure him, simply endure him. Now, even though his wound had probably deprived Gregor forever of the ability to move freely, and for the present it took him a very long time, like an aged invalid, merely to crawl across his room—climbing about at any height was entirely out of the question—this worsening of his condition was, in his opinion, amply compensated for by the following circumstance. The living-room door, which only an hour or two earlier he had constantly watched, was now left open, so that, lying in the darkness of his room and invisible from the living room, he was allowed to see the whole family gathered around the brightly lit table and, with their tacit sanction, as it were, to listen to their conversation in a way entirely different from before. Of course, what he heard was no longer the lively conversation of former days. In the past, whenever Gregor had been obliged to throw himself, utterly exhausted, into the damp bedding of some little hotel room, he had always thought of such conversations with a certain longing.

p.src: With a kind of obstinacy, his father refused to take off his attendant’s uniform even at home. His nightshirt hung uselessly from its hook, while he dozed in his place fully dressed in uniform, as though always ready for duty and expecting even at home to hear his superior’s summons. Gregor would often spend the whole evening looking at this uniform, which gleamed with its constantly polished gold buttons but was stained all over. Clad in such clothes, the old man slept in great discomfort, yet peacefully. As soon as the clock struck ten, his mother would softly wake his father and try to persuade him to go to bed. For the sleep he got there was not real sleep, and his father, who had to report for work at six, sorely needed proper rest. But with the obstinacy that had taken hold of him since he became an attendant, he would always insist on staying at the table longer, though he invariably fell asleep again. Even then, it took tremendous effort to persuade him to exchange the chair for his bed. However much his mother and sister urged him on with brief admonitions, he would spend some fifteen minutes slowly shaking his head, his eyes closed, refusing to get up. His mother would tug at his sleeve and whisper coaxing words into his ear, while his sister abandoned her studies to help her mother, but none of this had any effect on him. He would sink ever deeper into his chair.

His mother took care of everything else alongside the great quantity of sewing she had to do. The members of the family had done, to the utmost limit, everything the world demands of poor people. His father carried breakfasts to minor bank employees, his mother sacrificed herself sewing underwear for strangers, and his sister, at the customers’ bidding, scurried back and forth behind the counter. But the family’s strength had already reached its limit. p.src: Gregor passed both night and day almost entirely without sleep. At times he thought that the next time the door opened, he would once again take all the family's affairs into his own hands, just as he had before. For the first time in ages, there appeared in his mind, one after another, the proprietor and the manager, the clerks and apprentices, the remarkably dim-witted office boy, two or three friends from other firms, a chambermaid at a country hotel—a pleasant, fleeting memory—and a girl who worked the till in a milliner's shop, whom he had courted earnestly but far too leisurely. —All of them appeared mingled among strangers and people he had long since forgotten. Yet none of them would help him or his family; they were all beyond his reach, and Gregor was glad when they disappeared. But then he would lose all inclination to concern himself with his family. His heart would be filled only with anger at the inadequacy of their care. Although he could not imagine anything he wanted to eat, he devised all sorts of plans for getting into the kitchen and taking whatever might suit him, even if he was not at all hungry. His sister no longer gave any thought to what might especially please Gregor; before leaving for the shop in the morning and at noon, she would hurriedly push some food that happened to be on hand into his room with her foot. In the evening, without caring whether the food had perhaps been merely tasted or—as was most often the case—left entirely untouched, she would sweep it out of the room with a single stroke of the broom.

p.src: His sister now always cleaned the room in the evening, and she did it so carelessly that it could scarcely have been finished any faster. Streaks of grime ran along all four walls, while heaps of dust and filth lay scattered here and there. At first, whenever his sister came in, Gregor would station himself in one of the corners where the dirt was especially conspicuous, intending, as it were, to reproach her by his posture. But even if he remained there for weeks, his sister would surely never mend her ways. She saw the dirt just as clearly as he did, but she had resolved to leave it there. At the same time, with a touchiness new to her, though by then it had seized the entire family, she remained vigilant that the cleaning of Gregor's room should still be regarded as her responsibility. On one occasion, his mother undertook a thorough cleaning of Gregor's room. She managed to complete the cleaning with no more than two or three buckets of water. —The soaking wet room had, to be sure, put Gregor in a bad temper, and he sat broad and motionless on the sofa in sullen indignation—but his mother did not escape punishment for it. For that evening, as soon as his sister noticed the change in Gregor's room, she felt deeply affronted, rushed into the living room, and, despite her mother's raised hands and entreaties, began to weep, trembling all over. Her parents—her father, of course, had started up in alarm from his armchair—at first stared at her, startled and helpless, but at last they too began to act.

p.src: By now, Gregor was eating almost nothing at all. Only when he happened to pass the food that had been set out for him would he playfully take a morsel into his mouth, keep it there for hours, and then usually spit it out again. At first, he had thought that grief over the state of his room was keeping him from eating, but he soon grew accustomed to the various changes in it. It had become customary to put in his room anything that could not be stored elsewhere, and there were many such things. This was because one of the rooms in the apartment had been let to three male lodgers. These solemn gentlemen—all three of whom, as Gregor once confirmed through a crack in the door, wore full beards—were extremely fond of order, not only in their own room but, now that they were lodging in this household, throughout the entire apartment, and especially in the kitchen. They could not tolerate unnecessary objects or dirty clutter. Moreover, they had brought most of their own furnishings with them. As a result, many household items had become unnecessary, but they could neither be sold nor could the family bring themselves to throw them away. All these things were moved into Gregor's room. That was how the ash bin and the rubbish bin made their way there from the kitchen. Whatever was not needed for the moment was simply flung into Gregor's room by the charwoman, who was always in a tremendous hurry. Fortunately, Gregor usually saw only the object being brought in and the hand holding it.

p.src: The lodgers sometimes took their evening meal at home in the common sitting room. Consequently, the sitting-room door remained closed on many evenings. But Gregor quite readily resigned himself to not having the door opened. Even on many evenings when the door stood open, he did not take full advantage of it, but lay unnoticed by his family in the darkest corner of his room. One evening, however, the old charwoman left the door leading to the sitting room slightly ajar. It was still open when the lodgers came in that evening and the light was switched on. The three men sat down at the head of the table. It was where Gregor and his father and mother had once sat. Then the three unfolded their napkins and took up their knives and forks. His mother soon appeared in the doorway carrying a dish of meat, followed immediately by his sister with a heaping dish of potatoes. The food was sending up clouds of steam. As though intending to inspect the food before eating it, the lodgers bent over the dishes set before them. And indeed, the man sitting in the middle, who seemed to command a certain authority over the other two, cut off a piece of meat on the platter. He apparently wanted to make sure that it was tender enough and would not have to be sent back to the kitchen. But the man was satisfied, and Gregor's mother and sister, who had been watching tensely, breathed sighs of relief and began to smile. The family themselves ate in the kitchen. Even so, before going into the kitchen, Gregor's father entered this room, bowed once, then walked all the way around the table with his uniform cap in his hand. The lodgers all rose and muttered something into their beards.

p.src: The moment he entered his room, the door was hurriedly slammed shut behind him, securely bolted, and sealed off. The sudden loud noise behind him startled Gregor so badly that his little legs gave way beneath him. It was his sister who had acted with such haste. She had already risen and stood waiting, then darted forward in an instant. Gregor had not heard his sister approaching at all. As she turned the key in the lock, she cried, “At last!” his sister cried. “And now?” Gregor asked himself, looking around in the darkness. Before long, he discovered that he could no longer move at all. That did not strike him as strange. What seemed unnatural, rather, was that until now he had actually managed to drag his body along on those frail little legs. All things considered, he felt relatively comfortable. True, his whole body ached, but it seemed that the pain was gradually weakening and would ultimately disappear altogether. He could scarcely feel the rotten apple in his back, now completely covered with soft dust, or the inflamed area around it. He thought of his family with tenderness and love. His conviction that he must disappear was perhaps even firmer than his sister’s. He remained in this state of empty, peaceful contemplation until at last the tower clock struck three in the morning. He was still aware of the world outside the window beginning to grow light. Then, against his will, his head sank down completely. His final breath escaped faintly from his nostrils.
